s.dp: Discourse Referentials › Speaker
s.d: a reference to the speaker (with an added feature of emphasis in the form ἐγώ)
s.c: The terminology ‘first, second, and third persons’ reflects the normal order in Greek in which the so-called first person always occurred first in any listing of participants. The second person would be in the second position, and similarly, the third person would be in a third relative position. To preserve that order in English, however, could imply impoliteness, and it is for that reason that it is preferable to translate ⟦John 10:30|John 10:30⟧ as ‘the Father and I are one.’

s.dp: Discourse Referentials › Speaker and Those Associated with the Speaker [exclusive and inclusive]
s.d: a reference to the speaker or writer and those associated with him or her, either including or excluding the audience (with an added feature of emphasis in the form ἡμεῖς)

s.dp: Be, Become, Exist, Happen › State
s.d: to possess certain characteristics, whether inherent or transitory
s.c: In some expressions, the verb εἰμί is absent, e.g. μακάριοι οἱ δοῦλοι ἐκεῖνοι ‘truly fortunate are those servants’ ⟦Luke 12:37|Luke 12:37⟧.

s.dp: Be, Become, Exist, Happen › State
s.d: to be identical with

s.dp: Be, Become, Exist, Happen › Exist
s.d: to exist, in an absolute sense

s.dp: Be, Become, Exist, Happen › Happen
s.d: to occur, of an event

s.dp: Existence in Space › Be in a Place
s.d: to be in a place

s.dp: Mode › Possible, Impossible
s.d: to mark an event as being possible in a highly generic sense
s.c: In ⟦Hebrews 9:5|Hebrews 9:5⟧ one cannot determine precisely those factors which make it impossible for the author to be more precise. It may be simply the urgency of other matters or the limitations of space or even the inappropriateness of such considerations for the topic under consideration. In some languages, however, one must be somewhat more specific, for a strictly literal translation might imply that the author of the Epistle to the Hebrews was simply incapable of producing a detailed analysis. This would, of course, be quite contradictory to the implication of the statement in ⟦Hebrews 9:5|Hebrews 9:5⟧ and the scope of the wider context.

s.dp: Nature, Class, Example › Archetype, Corresponding Type [Antitype]
s.d: to belong to a particular class
s.c: In ⟦John 1:1|John 1:1⟧ θεός obviously is a unique member of a class, and therefore syntactically this would appear to be a case of complete identification. One can, however, translate ‘the Word was God’ but not ‘God was the Word.’

s.dp: Nature, Class, Example › Archetype, Corresponding Type [Antitype]
s.d: to correspond to something else in certain significant features
s.g: to correspond to; to stand for; to be a figure of; to represent

s.dp: Be, Become, Exist, Happen › Change of State
s.d: to change from one state to another

s.dp: Association › Associate
s.d: (an idiom, literally: to be in the bosom of) to be closely and intimately associated, with the implication of strong affection for
s.g: to be closely involved with; to be close beside
s.c: In ⟦John 1:18|John 1:18⟧ one may speak of the Son as ‘being at the Father’s side’ or ‘being in closest communion with the Father.’

s.dp: Aspect › Continue
s.d: (an idiom, literally: to be in) to continue to perform certain activities with care and concern
s.g: to practice; to continue to do; to cultivate
s.c: The construction in ⟦1 Timothy 4:15|1 Timothy 4:15⟧, in which ταῦτα μελέτα and ἐν τούτοις ἴσθι appear to be essentially synonymous reinforcements one of the other, would appear to fully justify combining these expressions as essentially equivalent in meaning, but for another interpretation of μελετάω in ⟦1 Timothy 4:15|1 Timothy 4:15⟧, see LN 30.20.

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Live, Die
s.d: (an idiom, literally: to be in death) to be in imminent danger of dying
s.g: to face death; to be likely to die

s.dp: Status › High Status or Rank [including persons of high status]
s.d: (an idiom, literally: to be someone) to be an important person
s.g: to be great; to be important

s.dp: Status › Slave, Free
s.d: (an idiom, literally: to be under a yoke) to be in a state of slavery
s.c: In ⟦1 Timothy 6:1|1 Timothy 6:1⟧ ὑπὸ ζυγὸν is redundant in that it simply emphasizes the status of being a slave.

s.dp: Relations › Equivalence
s.d: a marker of an explanation or a clarification in the same or a different language
s.c: In some languages one must make more specific the interpretation of a term in another language. For example, in ⟦Mark 3:17|Mark 3:17⟧ it may be necessary to translate ‘Boanerges, which in another language means Men of Thunder’ or ‘Boanerges, for which we would say, Men of Thunder.’

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Live, Die
s.d: (an idiom, literally: to be in a dwelling, see {D:7.8}) to be alive, with special emphasis upon physical existence on earth
s.c: Most languages have rather generic expressions for ‘life’ or ‘to live,’ but sometimes there are idiomatic expressions which may readily fit the types of contexts illustrated by ⟦2 Corinthians 5:6|2 Corinthians 5:6⟧ and ⟦2 Peter 1:13|2 Peter 1:13⟧, for example, ‘to have strength,’ ‘to have one’s eyes,’ and ‘to walk about on the earth.’

s.dp: Hold a View, Believe, Trust › Suppose, Think Possible
s.d: to form ideas which are unrelated to reality, normally with a negative connotation
s.c: It is also possible to understand ἐκζήτησις in ⟦1 Timothy 1:4|1 Timothy 1:4⟧ as meaning ‘controversies’ or ‘arguments’ (see LN 33.442).

s.dp: Communication › Dispute, Debate
s.d: a dispute involving empty speculation
s.c: For another interpretation of ἐκζήτησις in ⟦1 Timothy 1:4|1 Timothy 1:4⟧, see LN 31.33.

s.dp: Learn › Try To Learn
s.d: attempting to learn something by careful investigation or searching
s.c: The clause ‘about how I could get information on these matters’ (⟦Acts 25:20|Acts 25:20⟧) may also be rendered as ‘about how I should try to find out about these matters’ or ‘about how I could learn about these matters.’

s.dp: Communication › Dispute, Debate
s.d: expressing of forceful differences of opinion without necessarily having a presumed goal of seeking a solution

s.dp: Attitudes and Emotions › Surprise, Astonish
s.d: to wonder greatly or to be very much amazed

s.dp: Attitudes and Emotions › Surprise, Astonish
s.d: (derivative of {L:θαῦμα<SDBG:θαῦμα:000000>}[a] ‘wonder, amazement,’ {D:25.212}) to wonder or marvel at some event or object
s.g: to wonder; to be amazed; to marvel (whether the reaction is favorable or unfavorable depends on the context)

s.dp: Communication › Flatter
s.d: (an idiom, literally: to admire the face) to praise someone, normally in an exaggerated or false manner and with insincere purpose{N:001}

s.dp: Features of Objects › Hot, Lukewarm, Cold
s.d: pertaining to being hot, often associated with boiling
s.c: In ⟦Revelation 3:15|Revelation 3:15⟧ the usage is figurative; ζεστός in the sense of a favorable attitude towards something seems not to have been a conventionalized meaning.|In a number of languages the contrast between ‘hot’ and ‘cold’ may refer primarily to sex or anger, in which case the contrast is certainly not appropriate for ⟦Revelation 3:15|Revelation 3:15⟧. It may therefore be necessary in many instances to use an equivalent such as ‘for or against’ or ‘friendly to or hostile toward.’

s.dp: Number › Pair, Group [Numbered Collectives]
s.d: a collective of two

s.dp: Artifacts › Instruments Used in Binding and Fastening
s.d: an instrument for joining together objects (normally two)
s.c: In ⟦Acts 27:40|Acts 27:40⟧ ζευκτηρία refers to ropes employed in linking two rudders of a boat. In most languages, however, one would simply use a term for ‘rope.’

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: the chief Greek deity

s.dp: Attitudes and Emotions › Be Eager, Be Earnest, In a Devoted Manner
s.d: (an idiom, literally: to boil in the spirit) to show great eagerness toward something
s.g: to show enthusiasm; to commit oneself completely to
s.c: In some languages it may be difficult to find an appropriate equivalent of the phrase ‘with great enthusiasm,’ but in some instances an equivalent expression may be ‘he showed how much he liked to do’ or ‘he showed how he did so with all his heart.’

s.dp: Attitudes and Emotions › Be Eager, Be Earnest, In a Devoted Manner
s.d: to be deeply committed to something, with the implication of accompanying desire
s.g: to be earnest; to set one’s heart on; to be completely intent upon

s.dp: Attitudes and Emotions › Be Eager, Be Earnest, In a Devoted Manner
s.d: to be deeply committed to something, with the implication of accompanying desire
s.g: to be earnest; to set one’s heart on; to be completely intent upon
s.c: It is also possible to understand ζηλοῦτε in ⟦1 Corinthians 12:31|1 Corinthians 12:31⟧ as being indicative and therefore translated as ‘you set your hearts on the more important gifts.’

s.dp: Attitudes and Emotions › Love, Affection, Compassion
s.d: to have a deep concern for or devotion to someone or something
s.g: to have a deep concern for; to be devoted to; earnest concern
s.c: The Judaizers referred to in ⟦Galatians 4:17|Galatians 4:17⟧ may have been sincere, but they were misguided in their zeal.

s.dp: Attitudes and Emotions › Desire Strongly
s.d: set one’s heart on something that belongs to someone else
s.c: It is, of course, also possible to render ζηλόω in ⟦James 4:2|James 4:2⟧ as meaning ‘to be envious’ or ‘to be jealous’ (see LN 88.163).

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Envy, Jealousy
s.d: to experience strong envy and resentment against someone
s.g: to be jealous; to be envious

s.dp: Attitudes and Emotions › Love, Affection, Compassion
s.d: having a deep concern for or devotion to someone or something

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Envy, Jealousy
s.d: a particularly strong feeling of resentment and jealousy against someone

s.dp: Degree › Much, Little [Positive-Negative Degree]
s.d: a high point on a scale of extent and implying intensity of involvement

s.dp: Attitudes and Emotions › Be Eager, Be Earnest, In a Devoted Manner
s.d: one who is deeply committed to something and therefore zealous

s.dp: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes › Socio-Political
s.d: a member of a Jewish nationalistic group seeking independence from Rome
s.c: It is possible that ζηλωτής in ⟦Luke 6:15|Luke 6:15⟧ and Καναναῖος in ⟦Matthew 10:4|Matthew 10:4⟧ function not so much as a designation of an individual belonging to the particular Jewish nationalistic party (according to some scholars such a party may not have been organized at that time), but of one whjo is simply zealous for national independence (see ζηλωτής ‘enthusiast, zealous person,’ LN 25.77). Therefore, one might speak of Simon as ‘Simon the patriot’ (the same applies to ⟦Acts 1:13|Acts 1:13⟧, the only other occurrence of ζηλωτής in the NT). To render ζηλωτής as ‘armed insurrectionist’ or ‘guerilla fighter’ (as some translators have suggested) would be reading into the text more than is specifically warranted.

s.dp: Possess, Transfer, Exchange › Take, Obtain, Gain, Lose
s.d: suffering the loss of something which one has previously possessed, with the implication that the loss involves considerable hardship or suffering{N:001}

s.dp: Possess, Transfer, Exchange › Take, Obtain, Gain, Lose
s.d: to suffer the loss of something which one has previously possessed, with the implication that the loss involves considerable hardship or suffering{N:001}

s.dp: Punish, Reward › Punish
s.d: to be punished, with the implication of suffering damage
s.g: to be punished; to suffer punishment
s.c: It is also possible to understand ζημιόομαι in ⟦1 Corinthians 3:15|1 Corinthians 3:15⟧ as meaning simply ‘to suffer loss’ (see LN 57.69).

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: a Christian lawyer

s.dp: Learn › Try To Learn
s.d: to try to learn the location of something, often by movement from place to place in the process of searching
s.g: to try to learn where something is; to look for; to try to find

s.dp: Learn › Try To Learn
s.d: to attempt to learn something by careful investigation or searching
s.g: to try to learn; to search; to try to find out; to seek information

s.dp: Attitudes and Emotions › Desire, Want, Wish
s.d: to desire to have or experience something, with the probable implication of making an attempt to realize one’s desire{N:001}

s.dp: Communication › Ask For, Request
s.d: to ask for something which is being especially sought
s.g: to ask earnestly for; to demand
s.c: For another interpretation of ζητέω in ⟦Mark 8:11|Mark 8:11⟧, see LN 57.59.

s.dp: Aspect › Try, Attempt
s.d: to seek to do something, but without success
s.g: to seek to do; to try

s.dp: Be, Become, Exist, Happen › State
s.d: to attempt to attain some state or condition
s.g: to attempt to find; to try to be

s.dp: Possess, Transfer, Exchange › Take, Obtain, Gain, Lose
s.d: to try to obtain something from someone
s.g: to try to obtain; to attempt to get; to seek
s.c: For another interpretation of ζητέω in ⟦Mark 8:11|Mark 8:11⟧, see LN 33.167.

s.dp: Violence, Harm, Destroy, Kill › Kill
s.d: (an idiom, literally: to seek the life) to desire or intend to kill
s.g: to want to kill; to desire to kill

s.dp: Communication › Dispute, Debate
s.d: expressing of forceful differences of opinion without necessarily having a presumed goal of seeking a solution

s.dp: Plants › Plants That Are Not Trees
s.d: a particularly undesirable weed resembling wheat and possessing a seed which is poisonous
s.c: In this one passage in which ζιζάνιον occurs in the NT, it is possible to use an expression such as ‘poisonous weed’ or ‘bad weed.’

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: a governor in postexilic Jerusalem who was mentioned in the genealogy of Jesus

s.dp: Physical Events and States › Darkness
s.d: a condition of darkness associated with feelings of despair and foreboding
s.c: In ⟦Hebrews 12:18|Hebrews 12:18⟧ γνόφος ‘darkness’ (LN 14.53) and ζόφος may be combined to form a phrase such as ‘fearful darkness’ or ‘darkness that causes fear’ or ‘fear because of darkness.’

s.dp: Geographical Objects and Features › Regions Below the Surface of the Earth
s.d: (an idiom, literally: the gloom of darkness) the dark, gloomy nature of hell as a place of punishment

s.dp: Artifacts › Instruments Used in Agriculture and Husbandry
s.d: a bar or frame of wood by which two draft animals are joined at the head or neck in order to work together effectively in pulling a plow, harrow, or wagon
s.c: ζυγός occurs in the NT only in figurative contexts. In a sense, this means that ζυγός is itself figurative in meaning, but the figure of speech is an extended figure in which case individual components are normally regarded as having a literal meaning.

s.dp: Artifacts › Instruments for Measuring
s.d: an instrument for weighing objects
s.c: A balance scale may be described in some languages as ‘a tool for weighing’ or ‘an instrument for knowing how much something weighs.’ Ancient balance scales often consisted of a rod held by a cord in the middle and with pans attached to both ends. Weights could be placed in one pan, while the item to be weighed would be placed in the other.

s.dp: Foods and Condiments › Food
s.d: leaven employed in making bread rise
s.c: In some languages yeast is described simply as ‘that which makes bread rise,’ but frequently yeast is described in terms of some characteristic or on the basis of its source, for example, ‘sour froth’ or ‘beer foam.’

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Hypocrisy, Pretense
s.d: (a figurative extension of meaning of {L:ζύμη<SDBG:ζύμη:000000>}[a] ‘yeast,’ {D:5.11}) hypocritical behavior, probably implying hidden attitudes and motivations
s.c: In ⟦Matthew 16:6|Matthew 16:6⟧ the ζύμη of the Pharisees and the Sadducees is equated with their teaching, but the context would indicate clearly that this was a type of hypocritical teaching, since the religious leaders said one thing but did something quite different.|In ⟦1 Corinthians 5:6|1 Corinthians 5:6⟧, ⟦1 Corinthians 5:7|1 Corinthians 5:7⟧ there is an extended figurative reference to ζύμη. At first, ζύμη must be understood in the literal sense (as in Domain 5), yet ζύμη in verse 7 refers to wrong behavior. It is important, however, to try to preserve the continuity of the figurative reference, and for that reason the phrase παλαιὰ ζύμη is sometimes translated as ‘the old yeast of sin.’ It is difficult to know to what extent there may be a reference at this point to the hypocrisy which accompanies legalistic behavior.

s.dp: Foods and Condiments › Food
s.d: (derivative of {L:ζύμη<SDBG:ζύμη:000000>} ‘yeast,’ {D:5.11}) to employ yeast in the process of making bread rise

s.dp: Control, Rule › Control, Restrain
s.d: to bring under control and to continue to restrain
s.g: to control; to bring under control; to hold in check
s.c: In many languages it may be difficult to speak of ‘bringing a person under control.’ It may therefore be more appropriate to use some such phrase as ‘not allow a person to do just what he wants’ or ‘make a person behave’ or ‘make a person obey.’ In speaking of animals, one may render ⟦James 3:7|James 3:7⟧ as ‘all kinds of wild animals … can be made to obey a person.’

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Live, Die
s.d: the condition of being alive and well because of the presence of air to breathe and food to eat; in many cases its usage implies health, strength, and some degree of prosperity
s.c: In some figurative expressions ζάω and ζωή may involve serious complications in reference. For example, in ⟦John 6:51|John 6:51⟧ the expression ἐγώ εἰμι ὁ ἄρτος ὁ ζῶν ‘I am the living bread’ may be understood in some languages as bread which has some living objects in it, namely, bread which is being eaten by worms or weevils. It may therefore be necessary to say ‘I am that bread which gives life.’|In ⟦Mark 10:30|Mark 10:30⟧, καὶ ἐν τῷ αἰῶνι τῷ ἐρχομένῳ ζωὴν αἰώνιον ‘and in the age to come (he will receive) eternal life,’ there are significant differences of opinion as to whether the emphasis is primarily upon duration or upon the quality of life which is to be characteristic of the coming age. Since in some languages life can only be spoken of as a verb meaning literally ‘to live,’ then ‘eternal life’ might be expressed merely as ‘living without dying,’ but this can be misunderstood to mean that Christians will never die physically. Some translators have thus spoken of ‘eternal life’ as being ‘real life that never ends.’ In this way a qualitative distinction is introduced so that readers will not think merely in terms of the prolongation of earthly life, something which in some parts of the world would be regarded as being a terrible punishment rather than a blessing.|In a number of languages there is no noun-like word for ‘life.’ It may therefore be necessary to change all passages which speak of ‘life’ into a corresponding expression using a verb-like form meaning ‘to live.’

s.dp: Artifacts › Cloth, Leather, and Objects Made of Such Materials
s.d: a band of leather or cloth worn around the waist outside of one’s clothing
s.c: A ζώνη was normally quite wide and could be readily folded. As such, it was often used to carry money (see ⟦Matthew 10:9|Matthew 10:9⟧).

s.dp: Activities Involving Clothing and Adorning
s.d: to tuck up or hold a garment firmly in place by wrapping a belt, girdle, or piece of cloth around it{N:001}
s.g: to gird; to fasten one’s belt; to wear a narrow band of cloth around the waist; to tie around the waist

s.dp: Activities Involving Clothing and Adorning
s.d: to dress oneself, including the fastening of one’s belt as the final act in dressing

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Live, Die
s.d: to cause to continue to live
s.g: to keep alive; to preserve alive
s.c: ‘So that they could not be kept alive’ (⟦Acts 7:19|Acts 7:19⟧) may be rendered as ‘so that they would not continue to live’ or ‘so that they would die.’

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Live, Die
s.d: to cause to live
s.g: to give life to; to make live

s.dp: Animals
s.d: any living creature, whether wild or domesticated (in contrast with plants)
s.c: In a number of languages the equivalent of ‘living things’ or ‘living creatures’ is simply ‘those which are alive’ or ‘those that move about.’ ζῷον, therefore, includes essentially quadrupeds, fish, birds, and insects, and is not used in the NT to designate human beings. In several passages in the book of Revelation, ζῷον ‘a living being’ (LN 12.32) is employed to refer to supernatural beings at God’s throne (note ⟦Revelation 4:6|Revelation 4:6⟧ which in many ways is similar to the description of ‘living creatures’ in ⟦Ezekiel 1:5|Ezekiel 1:5⟧f).

s.dp: Supernatural Beings and Powers › Supernatural Beings
s.d: a supernatural being surrounding the throne of God in visions of the book of Revelation
s.c: The OT parallel for the ζῷον in Revelation is to be found in ⟦Ezekiel 1:5|Ezekiel 1:5⟧-⟦Ezekiel 1:14|Ezekiel 1:14⟧.

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Live, Die
s.d: to cause to live
s.g: to give life to; to make live

s.dp: Relations › Alternative Relation
s.d: a marker of an alternative

s.dp: Comparison
s.d: a marker of comparison

s.dp: Relations › Alternative Relation
s.d: a marker of double alternatives

s.dp: Control, Rule › Rule, Govern
s.d: (derivative of {L:ἡγεμών<SDBG:ἡγεμών:000000>}[a] ‘ruler,’ {D:37.59}) to be a governor, in the NT restricted to the meaning of a governor of a Roman province
s.c: The expression ‘Quirinius was governor of Syria’ (⟦Luke 2:2|Luke 2:2⟧) may be rendered in some languages as ‘Quirinius was the one who commanded all those in the province of Syria’ or ‘Quirinius gave orders to all those in Syria.’

s.dp: Control, Rule › Rule, Govern
s.d: ruling over, with the implication of providing direction and leadership
s.c: In a number of languages it may be necessary to express the concept of ‘ruling’ by some form of ‘command,’ for example, ‘he commands people what they must do’ or ‘he orders people’ or ‘he is the chief over people.’

s.dp: Control, Rule › Rule, Govern
s.d: (derivative of {L:ἡγέομαι<SDBG:ἡγέομαι:000002>}[c] ‘to rule,’ {D:37.58}) one who rules, with the implication of preeminent position
s.c: In the context of ⟦Matthew 2:6|Matthew 2:6⟧ it is possible to understand ‘rulers’ as a figurative reference to important places, and therefore one may also translate ‘you are by no means the least among the leading cities of Judah.’

s.dp: Control, Rule › Rule, Govern
s.d: (the Greek equivalent of the Latin term praefectus) a person who ruled over a minor Roman province

s.dp: Hold a View, Believe, Trust › Have an Opinion, Hold a View
s.d: to hold a view or have an opinion with regard to something
s.g: to hold a view; to have an opinion; to consider; to regard

s.dp: Guide, Discipline, Follow › Guide, Lead
s.d: to so influence others as to cause them to follow a recommended course of action
s.g: to guide; to direct; to lead
s.c: In some languages it is difficult to distinguish readily between expressions for ‘leading’ and those which refer to ‘ruling’ or ‘governing,’ but it is important to try to distinguish clearly between these two different sets of interpersonal relations. In some languages, the concept of ‘leading’ can be expressed by ‘showing how to’ or ‘demonstrating how one ought to.’ In other languages it is possible to speak of ‘leading’ as simply ‘going ahead of,’ but too often such an expression may designate only ‘a scout’ who goes ahead to see whether things are safe, or it may refer only to a person who insists on his prerogative as the most distinguished person in a group.

s.dp: Control, Rule › Rule, Govern
s.d: to rule over, with the implication of providing direction and leadership
s.g: to rule over; to order; to govern
s.c: In a number of languages it may be necessary to express the concept of ‘ruling’ by some form of ‘command,’ for example, ‘he commands people what they must do’ or ‘he orders people’ or ‘he is the chief over people.’

s.dp: Attitudes and Emotions › Happy, Glad, Joyful
s.d: pertaining to experiencing happiness, based primarily upon the pleasure derived

s.dp: Time › A Point of Time with Reference to Other Points of Time: Before, Long Ago, Now, At the Same Time, When, About, After
s.d: a point of time preceding another point of time and implying completion
s.c: Note that the subsequent point of time in ⟦Luke 11:7|Luke 11:7⟧ and ⟦Matthew 3:10|Matthew 3:10⟧ is the act of speaking.

s.dp: Time › A Point of Time with Reference to Other Points of Time: Before, Long Ago, Now, At the Same Time, When, About, After
s.d: (an idiom, literally: already sometime) a time simultaneous with the discourse but in relationship to preceding time
s.g: already now; now at last; now at length

s.dp: Attitudes and Emotions › Enjoy, Take Pleasure In, Be Fond of Doing
s.d: that which someone is fond of doing, in that it produces enjoyment

s.dp: Attitudes and Emotions › Desire Strongly
s.d: desire for physical pleasure, often sexual

s.dp: Plants › Plants That Are Not Trees
s.d: fragrant plant (genus Mentha); up to 2 m high; small, soft leaves with sawlike margins; used in cooking, tea, medicine
s.c: In designating ‘mint’ as well as ἄνηθον ‘dill,’ πήγανον ‘rue,’ and κύμινον ‘cumin,’ it is probably wise to borrow a term and use a classifier, for example, ‘a seasoning herb called mint.’

s.dp: Behavior and Related States › Custom, Tradition
s.d: a pattern of behavior more or less fixed by tradition and generally sanctioned by the society
s.c: In a number of languages there is no noun for ‘custom’ or ‘habit,’ but the same meaning is communicated by verbal aspects or adverbial phrases indicating habitual action. For example, in the case of ⟦John 19:40|John 19:40⟧ one may translate in some languages ‘as is the way in which Jews always bury people,’ and for ⟦1 Corinthians 11:16|1 Corinthians 11:16⟧ one may translate ‘this is not what we constantly do.’

s.dp: Linear Movement › Come, Come To, Arrive
s.d: to move toward and to arrive at a point{N:001}
s.g: to come to; to reach; to arrive

s.dp: Existence in Space › Be in a Place
s.d: to be in a place, as the result of having arrived
s.g: to be here; to be there
s.c: For another interpretation of ἥκω in ⟦John 8:42|John 8:42⟧, see LN 15.84.

s.dp: Be, Become, Exist, Happen › Happen
s.d: to have come or to be present, with respect to some temporal reference point

s.dp: Supernatural Beings and Powers › Supernatural Beings
s.d: a Hebrew term meaning my God
s.c: For certain problems involved in rendering an expression such as ‘my God,’ see the discussion in LN 12.1.

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: a person in the genealogy of Jesus

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: a major OT prophet

s.dp: Time › Indefinite Units of Time: Age, Lifetime, Interval, Period
s.d: the period of time when a person is alive
s.c: In ⟦Matthew 6:27|Matthew 6:27⟧ ἡλικία may also denote height (see LN 81.4). If one understands ἡλικία in ⟦Matthew 6:27|Matthew 6:27⟧ as time, then obviously some adjustment needs to be made to the meaning of πῆχυς ‘cubit’ (LN 81.25). For many languages the most appropriate term is one which means ‘day,’ but it would also be possible to use some other unit of length if this would clearly imply an impossibility.

s.dp: Time › Indefinite Units of Time: Age, Lifetime, Interval, Period
s.d: the period of life when one is mature and at one’s prime{N:001}
s.c: Normally the phrase παρὰ καιρὸν ἡλικίας (⟦Hebrews 11:11|Hebrews 11:11⟧) would refer to a woman beyond menopause.

s.dp: Spacial Dimensions › High, Low, Deep
s.d: height as the dimension of stature of an animate object

s.dp: Features of Objects › Large, Small
s.d: an interrogative of size occurring in indirect questions
s.g: how extensive; how large; how small

s.dp: Degree › Much, Little [Positive-Negative Degree]
s.d: a relatively high point on a scale involving exclamation
s.g: how; very; how great; how much; intense; severe
s.c: In a number of languages an expression of high degree in an exclamation can only be reproduced as an expression of intensive degree in a non-exclamatory form. For example, the statement in ⟦Matthew 6:23|Matthew 6:23⟧ ‘how great must the darkness be!’ must be rendered in a number of languages as ‘the darkness is very, very intense’ or ‘it is very, very dark there.’|In a number of languages the equivalent of ἡλίκον ἀγῶνα ἔχω in ⟦Colossians 2:1|Colossians 2:1⟧ would be ‘I struggle very much indeed.’

s.dp: Geographical Objects and Features › Heavenly Bodies
s.d: the large celestial body that gives warmth and light to earth in the daytime
s.c: Translators have relatively few difficulties in obtaining a satisfactory term for the sun, though there may be a tendency in some languages to add some kind of honorific title to the word, for example, ‘our father the sun.’ Translators’ problems occur, however, with verbs describing the action or effect of the sun. For example, in ⟦Matthew 13:6|Matthew 13:6⟧, instead of speaking of ‘the sun rising,’ it may be more satisfactory to speak of ‘the sun shining’ or, in this particular context, possibly ‘when the sun was overhead’ or ‘by the time the sun had reached the sky.’ In ⟦Mark 13:24|Mark 13:24⟧ one can perhaps best render the meaning as ‘the sun will no longer shine’ or ‘… will cease shining.’

s.dp: Artifacts › Instruments Used in Binding and Fastening
s.d: a thin piece of metal (usually iron) sharpened on one end (in the NT used only in connection with nails employed in the crucifixion)
s.c: In a number of languages a distinction is made between relatively small nails and larger spikes; the latter would be appropriate in speaking of crucifixion.

s.dp: Time › Definite Units of Time: Year, Month, Week, Day, Hour
s.d: according to Hebrew reckoning (as reflected in the NT), a period of time beginning at sunset and ending at the following sunset

s.dp: Time › Definite Units of Time: Year, Month, Week, Day, Hour
s.d: the daylight period between sunrise and sunset (divided into twelve hours)

s.dp: Time › Indefinite Units of Time: Age, Lifetime, Interval, Period
s.d: an indefinite unit of time (whether grammatically singular or plural), but not particularly long (note the contrast with {L:αἰών<SDBG:αἰών:000000>}[a] ‘age,’ {D:67.143}, and {L:γενεά<SDBG:γενεά:000003>}[d] ‘age,’ {D:67.144})
s.c: In a number of languages there is no specific term such as ‘period’ referring to an indefinite extent of time. One can, however, render ⟦Luke 1:23|Luke 1:23⟧ as ‘when he no longer had to serve in the Temple’ or ‘when he had finished the days when he served in the Temple.’

s.dp: Physical Events and States › Light
s.d: the light of the day in contrast with the darkness of night (see {L:νύξ<SDBG:νύξ:000001>}[b] ‘night,’ {D:14.59}){N:001}
s.c: In order to focus attention upon the beginning of daylight, one may translate ⟦Luke 4:42|Luke 4:42⟧ as ‘when the sun began to shine’ or ‘when the sky began to become light’ or even ‘when it was no longer night.’|In some languages there is no noun for either ‘day’ or ‘daylight,’ but a verb expression may be employed which may be rendered literally as ‘to day’ or ‘to become day.’

s.dp: Courts and Legal Procedures › Court of Justice
s.d: a court of justice for determining guilt or innocence{N:002}
s.c: For languages which do not have technical terms for a court, it is usually possible to use some such phrase as ‘to be brought before a judge’ or ‘to have judges decide one’s case.’

s.dp: Time › Duration of Time without Reference to Points or Units of Time: Time, Spend Time, Always, Eternal, Old, Immediately, Young
s.d: (idioms, literally: day out of day, and: throughout day, respectively) a relatively long period of time
s.g: for a long time; for quite a while; day after day; every day

s.dp: Courts and Legal Procedures › Judge, Condemn, Acquit
s.d: (an idiom, literally: day of slaughter) a time of destructive judgment
s.c: The reference of the phrase ἡμέρᾳ σφαγῆς in ⟦James 5:5|James 5:5⟧ is the destructive judgment of God, but it is possible that σφαγῆς should be interpreted in a more literal sense of ‘destruction’ rather than mere condemnation.

s.dp: Time › Duration of Time without Reference to Points or Units of Time: Time, Spend Time, Always, Eternal, Old, Immediately, Young
s.d: (idioms, literally: forty days and forty nights, forty days, respectively) possibly a symbolic temporal expression denoting a relatively long period of time
s.c: Most translations render ἡμέρας τεσσεράκοντα καὶ νύκτας τεσσεράκοντα as either ‘forty days and forty nights’ or ‘forty days,’ though it is possible, in view of the symbolic meaning of the number ‘forty,’ that this expression is to be understood as meaning a long period of time.

s.dp: Time › Duration of Time without Reference to Points or Units of Time: Time, Spend Time, Always, Eternal, Old, Immediately, Young
s.d: (an idiom, literally: to advance in days) to be quite advanced in age

s.dp: Time › Duration of Time without Reference to Points or Units of Time: Time, Spend Time, Always, Eternal, Old, Immediately, Young
s.d: (expressions, literally: night and day, day and night, day and day, respectively) duration of time, either continuous or episodic, but without limits
s.g: day and night; always; constantly; continually

s.d: time in an eschatological frame, referring to a final judgment or to the coming of Christ
s.g: Day of the Lord; Judgment Day

s.dp: Time › A Point of Time with Reference to Other Points of Time: Before, Long Ago, Now, At the Same Time, When, About, After
s.d: (an idiom, literally: through days) a point of time subsequent to another point of time after an interval of a few days

s.dp: Discourse Referentials › Speaker and Those Associated with the Speaker [exclusive and inclusive]
s.d: pertaining to the speaker or writer and those associated with him or her, either including or excluding the audience
s.c: This meaning is also found as a variant reading: κατὰ τὸν ἡμέτερον νόμον ἐβουλήθημεν ἀνελεῖν ‘we wished to judge him according to our law’ ⟦Acts 24:6|Acts 24:6⟧ (apparatus).

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Live, Die
s.d: the state of being somewhere between life and death
s.c: One may render ‘half dead’ as ‘almost dead’ or ‘about to die.’

s.dp: Number › Half, Third, Fourth [Fractional Part]
s.d: one half of an object, series, or mass

s.dp: Time › Definite Units of Time: Year, Month, Week, Day, Hour
s.d: a period of half an hour

s.dp: Time › A Point of Time with Reference to Other Points of Time: Before, Long Ago, Now, At the Same Time, When, About, After
s.d: indefinite and multiple points of time, simultaneous with other corresponding points of time

s.dp: Comparison
s.d: an emphatic marker of comparison

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Gentleness, Mildness
s.d: pertaining to being gentle, with the implication of kindness

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: a person in the genealogy of Jesus

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Peaceful Behavior
s.d: pertaining to a quiet, peaceful existence or attitude

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: Herod I, known as Herod the Great

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: Herod Antipas, son of Herod I, who had John the Baptist executed

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: Herod Agrippa I, grandson of Herod I

s.dp: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes › Socio-Political
s.d: the political followers and adherents to Herod the Great and his family

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: a granddaughter of Herod I and wife of Herod Antipas

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: a person greeted in {S:04501601100004}

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: a major OT prophet

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: a son of Isaac and the elder twin brother of Jacob

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Treat Badly
s.d: to experience worse treatment
s.g: to be treated worse; to suffer more

s.dp: Hostility, Strife › Conquer
s.d: to experience defeat and subjection
s.g: to be defeated; to be conquered; to be controlled by
s.c: In a number of languages ‘to be defeated’ is simply ‘to be conquered.’ In some instances this is expressed as ‘to become the prisoner of’ or idiomatically ‘to be led away by.’

s.dp: Degree › More Than, Less Than [Comparative Degree]
s.d: a degree which is lower than what would be expected in the context

s.dp: Value › Good, Bad
s.d: pertaining to being less satisfactory than something else

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Tire, Rest
s.d: to be at rest, that is, not to be engaged in some activity

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Peaceful Behavior
s.d: to live in a quiet, peaceful, mild manner

s.dp: Communication › Keep Silent
s.d: to maintain a state of silence, with a possible focus upon the attitude involved
s.g: to say nothing; to remain quiet

s.dp: Trouble, Hardship, Relief, Favorable Circumstances › Favorable Circumstances or State
s.d: a state of undisturbed quietness and calm
s.c: ‘To earn their own living’ (⟦2 Thessalonians 3:12|2 Thessalonians 3:12⟧) is a rendering of an idiom which is literally ‘to eat their own bread’ (see LN 57.190). For an interpretation of ἡσυχία in ⟦2 Thessalonians 3:12|2 Thessalonians 3:12⟧ focusing on personal behavior, see LN 88.103.

s.dp: Communication › Keep Silent
s.d: act of maintaining a state of silence, with a possible focus upon the attitude involved

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Peaceful Behavior
s.d: act of living in a quiet, peaceful, mild manner
s.c: For another interpretation of ἡσυχία in ⟦2 Thessalonians 3:12|2 Thessalonians 3:12⟧, focusing on the circumstances involved, see LN 22.43.

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Peaceful Behavior
s.d: pertaining to a quiet, peaceful existence or attitude

s.dp: Relations › Alternative Relation
s.d: a marker of double alternatives

s.dp: Be, Become, Exist, Happen › State
s.d: a lack of attaining a desirable state or condition

s.dp: Physical Events and States › Sound
s.d: to produce a sound or noise not involving human speech
s.g: to produce a sound; to make noise
s.c: In translating χαλκὸς ἠχῶν it is usually desirable to employ a term which will more specifically refer to the sound of brass cymbals, for example, ‘resounding cymbal’ or ‘clanging cymbal.’

s.dp: Artifacts › Musical Instruments
s.d: (an idiom, literally: echoing brass, or: resounding brass) a gong made of brass
s.c: In a number of languages the equivalent of gong is ‘noisy metal’ or ‘reverberating metal’ or ‘echoing metal,’ but frequently translators have simply used an expression meaning ‘loud bell.’

s.dp: Physical Events and States › Sound
s.d: any type of sound, tone, or noise other than human speech
s.c: In a number of languages it will be essential to make a clear distinction between various types of sound referred to by ἦχος . The sounds of a cymbal, a trumpet, and the sea are very frequently referred to by entirely different terms.

s.dp: Communication › Inform, Announce
s.d: information concerning a person or an event

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: one of the twelve apostles; see also {D:93.227}

s.dp: Geographical Objects and Features › Bodies of Water
s.d: a generic collective term for all bodies of water (in this sense θάλασσα[a] is contrasted with the sky and the land)
s.c: This generic sense of θάλασσα may be expressed in some languages as ‘extensions of water’ or simply as ‘water.’ In other instances it may be necessary to employ a phrase such as ‘lakes and oceans,’ while in certain languages a term for ocean also has a generic sense of any extensive area of water.

s.dp: Geographical Objects and Features › Bodies of Water
s.d: a particular body of water, normally rather large
s.c: The use of θάλασσα to refer to a lake such as the Lake of Galilee (⟦Matthew 4:18|Matthew 4:18⟧; ⟦Mark 1:16|Mark 1:16⟧) or the Lake of Tiberias (⟦John 21:1|John 21:1⟧) reflects Semitic usage, in which all bodies of water from oceans to pools could be referred to by a single term. Normal Greek usage would employ λίμνη lake, pool (LN 1.72).|Many languages make a clear distinction between different types of bodies of water. The three principal bases for differentiation are (1) fresh, brackish, or salty, (2) relative size, that is, large versus small bodies of water, and (3) existence of an outlet. On the basis of this third type of distinction, a term to designate the Sea of Galilee would need to be different from that used in speaking of the Dead Sea, since the Sea of Galilee has an outlet while the Dead Sea does not. Considerable care must be exercised in the choice of terms for such bodies of water, since failure to select the right terms may result in serious distortion of geography and therefore considerable misunderstanding of the geographical setting of biblical events.

s.dp: Help, Care For › Care For, Take Care Of
s.d: to take care of, with the implication of cherishing and concern for
s.c: It may be useful in some instances to translate ‘and takes care of it’ in ⟦Ephesians 5:29|Ephesians 5:29⟧ as ‘and gives to his own body whatever is needed’ or ‘and does for himself whatever is necessary.’

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: the daughter-in-law of Judah in the genealogy of Jesus

s.dp: Attitudes and Emotions › Surprise, Astonish
s.d: (derivative of {L:θάμβος<SDBG:θάμβος:000000>} ‘astonishment,’ {D:25.208}) to experience astonishment as the result of some unusual event
s.g: to be astonished; to be startled; to be amazed

s.dp: Attitudes and Emotions › Surprise, Astonish
s.d: a state of astonishment due to both the suddenness and the unusualness of the phenomenon and with either a positive or a negative reaction

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Live, Die
s.d: (derivative of {L:θάνατος<SDBG:θάνατος:000000>}[a] ‘death,’ {D:23.99}) that which causes or produces death

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Live, Die
s.d: that which causes or produces death
s.c: The phrase ‘deadly poison’ may be rendered as ‘that which can cause death’ or ‘that which causes people to die.’

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Live, Die
s.d: the process of dying
s.c: In a number of languages clear distinctions are made in the use of terms for dying on the basis of the manner or circumstances of death. For example, one term may refer to death primarily as the result of old age, while another term may refer to death caused by sickness, and still other terms may be used for death caused by violence. Careful distinctions must be used in determining the choice of terms based on particular contexts.

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Sickness, Disease, Weakness
s.d: a widespread contagious disease, often associated with divine retribution

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Live, Die
s.d: (an idiom, literally: to be in death) to be in imminent danger of dying
s.g: to face death; to be likely to die

s.dp: Violence, Harm, Destroy, Kill › Kill
s.d: to deprive a person of life, with the implication of this being the result of condemnation by legal or quasi-legal procedures

s.dp: Aspect › Cease, Stop
s.d: (a figurative extension of meaning of {L:θανατόω<SDBG:θανατόω:000000>}[a] ‘to put to death,’ {D:20.65}) to cease completely from activity, with the implication of extreme measures taken to guarantee such a cessation{N:001}
s.g: to stop completely; to cease completely
s.c: It is possible that in rendering this expression in ⟦Romans 8:13|Romans 8:13⟧ one may desire to retain the figure of speech and therefore translate ‘if by the Spirit you put to death the works of the body.’

s.dp: Funerals and Burial
s.d: to bury a dead person

s.dp: Help, Care For › Care For, Take Care Of
s.d: (possibly an idiom, literally: to bury my father) to take care of one’s father until his death
s.g: to take care of a father; to provide for one’s father until his death

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: the father of Abraham in the genealogy of Jesus

s.dp: Attitudes and Emotions › Courage, Boldness
s.d: to have confidence and firmness of purpose in the face of danger or testing
s.g: to be courageous; to have courage; to be bold
s.c: In a number of languages ‘courage’ is rendered by an idiomatic expression, for example, ‘to not move,’ ‘to be deaf to threats,’ and ‘to have a heart like iron.’

s.dp: Attitudes and Emotions › Courage, Boldness
s.d: to have confidence and firmness of purpose in the face of danger or testing
s.g: to be courageous; to have courage; to be bold
s.c: In a number of languages ‘courage’ is rendered by an idiomatic expression, for example, ‘to not move,’ ‘to be deaf to threats,’ and ‘to have a heart like iron.’

s.dp: Attitudes and Emotions › Courage, Boldness
s.d: (an idiom, literally: to take courage) to become confident or courageous in the face of real or possible danger
s.g: to become confident; to take courage

s.dp: Attitudes and Emotions › Surprise, Astonish
s.d: a state of wonderment or amazement, usually with the implication of marveling

s.dp: Attitudes and Emotions › Surprise, Astonish
s.d: an event which causes someone to wonder or marvel
s.g: wonder; miracle; something to be wondered at

s.dp: Attitudes and Emotions › Surprise, Astonish
s.d: (derivative of {L:θαυμάζω<SDBG:θαυμάζω:000000>} ‘to be amazed,’ {D:25.213}) pertaining to that which causes or is worthy of amazement and wonder

s.dp: Attitudes and Emotions › Surprise, Astonish
s.d: (derivative of {L:θαυμάζω<SDBG:θαυμάζω:000000>} ‘to be amazed,’ {D:25.213}) pertaining to that which causes or is worthy of amazement and wonder

s.dp: Supernatural Beings and Powers › Supernatural Beings
s.d: a female deity
s.c: In some languages it may seem quite strange to attribute female sex to a divine being. However, one can almost always say ‘a woman god’ or ‘a spirit like a woman’ or ‘a spirit thought of as being like a woman.’
